analysis.one_liner: Caps the number of patents brand-name biologic makers can use to sue cheaper biosimilar competitors.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed the bill without a single dissenting vote in July 2026, but the House has taken no action and the bill sits waiting at the House desk.
analysis.plain_summary: Brand-name biologic drug makers often hold large bundles of patents and can sue a biosimilar competitor over many of them at once, dragging out court battles that keep cheaper copies off the market. This bill says that in most such lawsuits the brand-name maker can only assert up to 20 patents, and no more than 10 of the late-filed ones, though a court can raise the limit for good cause. Patents covering how a drug is used in treatment are excluded from the cap.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who take expensive biologic drugs, and the biosimilar companies trying to sell lower-priced versions of them. Fewer patents in a lawsuit means shorter, cheaper litigation, which makes it easier for biosimilars to reach the market and puts downward pressure on drug prices [S2, S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients paying high biologic drug prices

how_it_helps.text: Caps at 20 the number of patents a brand-name biologic maker can assert in a lawsuit against a biosimilar applicant, with no more than 10 being patents filed more than four years after the original drug was approved [S2, S3].
The limit kicks in when the biosimilar applicant completes the required information-sharing steps under the FDA approval pathway, rewarding companies that follow the process [S2, S3].
A court can raise the cap if the interest of justice or good cause requires it, such as when a biosimilar maker withholds required information or materially changes its product [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name biologic manufacturers, who would lose part of their ability to use large patent portfolios — sometimes called patent thickets — to delay biosimilar competition and keep monopoly prices for longer. Their argument in good faith is that patents protect the returns that fund research into costly biologic drugs.

drawbacks.text: The cap still allows up to 20 patents per lawsuit, and method-of-use patents are entirely excluded from the limit, so a determined brand-name maker retains substantial litigation tools; critics of patent thickets would call this a partial fix [S3].
Courts may increase the cap for good cause, adding flexibility that also gives litigants another issue to argue over [S3].
The bill applies only to biosimilar applications submitted after enactment, so existing disputes and already-pending applications are untouched [S3].
Brand-name makers contend that robust patent protection is what finances the high cost of developing biologics, and that weakening enforcement could reduce investment in new medicines.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to patients is real but gradual: shorter patent fights should mean biosimilars reach the market sooner and prices fall, though the 20-patent cap and the exemptions for method-of-use patents mean brand-name makers keep most of their arsenal. The cost falls on drug companies' litigation leverage and future revenue, not directly on taxpayers or consumers. It is a modest, targeted reform rather than a sweeping one, and it passed the Senate with no opposition, suggesting even supporters saw it as uncontroversial.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed the bill with amendments by unanimous consent on July 21, 2026, and the House received it and is holding it at the desk with no vote taken yet.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced by Sen. Cornyn on March 13, 2025, with three cosponsors split between the parties, and was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee [S1, S4, S5].
The Judiciary Committee ordered the bill reported with amendments favorably on April 3, 2025, and it was reported on April 10 and placed on the Senate calendar [S5].
The Senate passed the bill with amendments by unanimous consent on July 21, 2026 [S5].
The House received the bill the same day and has held it at the desk, taking no further action so far [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, brand-name biologic makers keep their full patent-litigation toolkit while the bill waits; patients benefit only if the House acts before the Congress ends.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a bipartisan Senate sponsor team (2 Democrats, 1 Republican cosponsoring a Republican lead) and cleared the Senate by unanimous consent, so no party division appears anywhere in the record.

industries.note: These companies use large patent portfolios to sue biosimilar competitors and delay cheaper versions of their drugs; the bill caps how many patents they can assert in a single lawsuit, shortening the road to competition and lower prices.
Fewer patents per lawsuit means cheaper, faster litigation and a clearer path to FDA approval and market entry, which lets them sell lower-priced copies to patients.
When biosimilars reach the market sooner, prices for expensive biologics tend to fall, lowering costs for patients, insurers, and employers.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has passed the Senate and now needs House action before the Congress ends in January 2027. Because it cleared the Senate without opposition and is relatively narrow, it could pass the House the same way, but bills held at the desk with no scheduled action often simply expire when the two-year Congress ends, forcing the process to start over.
